Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify imaging modalities that aid in the diagnosis of osteoporosis.
Review the indications for assessing bone mineral density, including risk factors for
osteoporosis.
Discuss methods for assessing bone health, including dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry.
Explain alternative and supplemental tools available to assess fragility fracture risk.
Overview
Osteoporosis has a high prevalence and increases the risk for fragility fractures.
A diagnosis of osteoporosis can be made via bone mineral density (BMD) testing and/or clinical
history.
The most common method of testing is dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA).

BMD values are interpreted via T-scores and Z-scores.
Alternative devices and supplemental tools are available to further quantify the risk for fragility
fracture.
The International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) publishes position statements on
BMD testing in adults1 and pediatric patients.2
Osteoporosis and Fragility Fractures
Osteoporosis is associated with a high prevalence, and the prevalence increases with age.
Osteoporosis is clinically important because it places individuals at risk for fragility fractures.

Osteoporosis and Fragility Fractures
Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disease. Osteoporosis is defined as a
decrease in bone strength because of altered bone quality and/or decreased BMD below
a specific lower limit of normal. Osteoporosis is associated with an increased risk for
fracture, including low-energy fractures. Between 2005 and 2010, 16.2% of adults older
than 65 years in the United States had osteoporosis.3 The prevalence of osteoporosis
was higher in adults older than 80 years (25.7%).3
Osteopenia is defined as decreased bone mineral strength that is not necessarily
associated with an increased risk for fracture. Low bone mass or osteopenia is present in
48.3% of adults older than 65 years in the United States.3 The term may be used
nonspecifically in imaging reports to describe generalized or focal decreased BMD;
however, a clear definition of osteopenia exists based on DEXA scan findings. According
to the ISCD, the terms low bone mass or low bone density are preferred over
osteopenia; however, many institutions use either term.
Osteoporosis is clinically important because it places individuals at risk for fragility
fracture. A fragility fracture is defined as a fracture that occurred in a setting that would
not typically cause a fracture, such as a fall from standing height, low-energy trauma, or
no history of trauma. This definition excludes fractures related to pathologic lesions or

2/22

osteomalacia. Fragility fractures have a considerable effect on morbidity and mortality in
older age groups.4
Osteoporosis also is clinically important in the preoperative assessment. Low bone
mineral density is associated with adverse outcomes after arthroplasty and spine
surgery. Low bone density may be independent risk factors for increased postoperative
pain and density-related complications, such as kyphosis, adjacent segment
degenerative disk disease, or hardware failure5-7 (Video 1)
Video 1 Emery SE: Preoperative bone health optimization, from Anderson PA, mod:
Secondary fracture prevention. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Indications for Assessment
The prevalence of osteoporosis is higher in certain groups, based on age, sex, or
comorbidities.
The ISCD has published guidelines on patients in whom BMD testing is indicated (Table 1).
Women Older Than 65 Years and Men Older Than 70 Years
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
3/22

Any woman older than 65 years and any man older than 70 years should undergo BMD
testing. The prevalence of osteoporosis and the incidence of fragility fractures is high enough
in this patient group to warrant routine testing.
Other Adults
Recommendations for other adults depend on history of prior fracture, medication history,
and other comorbidities.

Based on data from The International Society for Clinical Densitometry: 2019 ISCD Official
Positions: Adult. Indications for Bone Mineral Density (BMD) Testing). 2019. Available at:
https://iscd.org/learn/official-positions/adult-positions/. Accessed May 7, 2021.

Indications for Assessment
Examples of individuals who may require BMD testing include but are not limited to the
following: older adults with a low body weight, adults with a history of fragility fracture,
adults being treated with medications that affect BMD (eg, androgen deprivation
therapy), and adults with chronic conditions that affect BMD (eg, spinal cord injury).
Baseline BMD testing also is indicated for transgender and gender nonconforming
individuals before the initiation of hormone therapy.
Any adult in whom a diagnosis of osteoporosis or osteopenia would lead to treatment
should undergo BMD testing. For example, preoperative BMD testing should be
considered in individuals undergoing elective orthopaedic surgery if they are at risk for
low bone mass and require bone health optimization preoperatively.
Diagnosis of Osteoporosis
A diagnosis of osteoporosis can be made via BMD testing and/or clinical history.
Individuals with a history of fragility fracture are considered to have osteoporosis regardless of
the results of BMD testing.

Diagnosis of Osteoporosis
The National Bone Health Alliance published recommendations for the diagnosis of
osteoporosis,8 which include DEXA scan findings and clinical history (Table 2). These
criteria only apply to postmenopausal women and men older than 50 years.
DEXA is the most common imaging modality to assess for osteoporosis; however, a
diagnosis of osteoporosis is not solely based on DEXA scan findings. DEXA only evaluates
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
5/22

loss of BMD. Osteoporosis results from decreased bone density and/or altered bone
quality. An example of osteoporosis related to decreased bone quality is diabetes
mellitus–related osteoporosis. In individuals with diabetes mellitus, bone quality may be
considerably altered, and DEXA may not predict the full extent of fracture risk. Other
tools are used to better predict fracture risk based on decreased bone density and
factors that affect bone quality.

the prevalence of osteoporosis in the USA. Osteoporos Int 2016;28(4):1225-1232.
Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry
DEXA is the most common imaging modality to assess BMD.
DEXA is clinically accurate, reproducible, and performed with low radiation.

Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry
Osteoporosis may be suspected based on conventional radiographs, CT scans, or MRIs if
cortical thinning or loss of bony trabeculae is observed; however, these imaging studies
are not as sensitive or specific for the diagnosis of osteoporosis as DEXA scans.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
6/22

Ultimately, DEXA is considered the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of
osteoporosis.
Technique
A DEXA scanner emits low-dose radiation to assess BMD.
DEXA is commonly performed at the lumbar spine (L1 through L4) or the hip.
DEXA produces a low-quality frontal image of the site of assessment. This image is used to
determine the region of interest (ROI) in which BMD will be calculated.

Technique
A DEXA scanner is not equivalent to a conventional radiograph machine (Figure 1). A
DEXA scanner emits low-dose x-rays at two different energy spectrums. Bone will block
or attenuate the two x-ray beams differently, depending on the density. The scanner
calculates the density in grams per cm2 based on the difference in the two x-ray beams. 
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
7/22

Figure 1 Photograph shows an example of a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scanner.
The patient is placed in the supine position on the table, and the x-ray tube/detector is
moved into position to image the spine, hip, or forearm. (Courtesy of Rina Patel, MD, San
Francisco, CA.)
The sites of assessment are the lumbar spine (L1 through L4) and the proximal femur. If
imaging of one of these two sites is not feasible (eg, because of metal implants or severe
posttraumatic deformity or in patients over the weight limit of the scanner table), then
the forearm may be assessed. Assessment of the forearm also is helpful in individuals
with hyperparathyroidism.
The DEXA scanner produces a low-quality image of the lumbar spine, hip, or forearm.
The images are extremely limited and not of diagnostic quality. The purpose of the
images is to help define a ROI in which BMD will be calculated.
DEXA Report
The DEXA report includes calculated BMD, T-scores, and Z-scores.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
8/22

The T-score is the number of standard deviations that BMD varies from the mean in young
women.
The Z-score is the number of standard deviations that BMD varies from the mean in an age-,
race-, and sex-matched group.
T-scores and Z-scores are used to diagnose low BMD because these scores better predict the
risk for fragility fracture.

DEXA Report
The DEXA report shows the mean BMD at the lumbar spine, the BMD at the femoral
neck, and the BMD of the total (proximal) femur. The lowest of those three values
determines the diagnosis. The BMD measurement alone is not useful in assessing
fracture risk. The BMD values are compared with those of a young, female group (T-
scores) or matched group (Z-scores), which are better predictors of the risk for fracture.
The diagnosis of osteoporosis and osteopenia in postmenopausal women and in men
older than 50 years is based on T-scores. The reference database for T-scores is
Caucasian women aged 20 to 29 years. This reference is used for all patients, regardless
of race or sex. A T-score between –1.0 and –2.5 meets criteria for low BMD or osteopenia
(Figure 2). An individual with a T-score of less than –2.5 is diagnosed with osteoporosis
(Figure 3).
The interpretation of BMD in premenopausal women or in men younger than 50 years is
not as simple. In these patients, BMD alone does not meet the criteria for diagnosis of
osteoporosis or osteopenia. Instead, a Z-score of less than –2.0 is described as below
expected range for age. The reference database for Z-scores is matched to the patient’s
age, sex, and race. Clinical history, particularly history of fragility fracture, is used to
diagnose osteoporosis in premenopausal patients.9

Pitfalls and Limitations
DEXA is not foolproof. Errors in placement of the ROI may falsely increase or decrease the
calculated BMD.
DEXA only assesses one part of osteoporosis (decreased bone density) and does not account
for the fracture risk related to altered bone quality.
DEXA only assesses cortical bone.

Pitfalls and Limitations
The BMD calculated via DEXA may not be accurate. The most common cause for an
erroneous BMD is if the ROI is incorrect. In these situations, areas that are higher density
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
11/22

(eg, metal implants) or lower density (eg, bone cyst) than the surrounding bone may
falsely increase or decrease the measured BMD (Figure 3). Other recommendations that
guide the reporting of DEXA are outlined in the ISCD official positions.1
Decreased bone strength is a result of decreased bone density and/or altered bone
quality; however, DEXA only assesses decreased bone density. Therefore, DEXA does not
account for all the potential risk for fracture in an individual. In some individuals with
conditions that affect bone quality, such as diabetes mellitus, DEXA may not accurately
predict fracture risk. The Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) is one of the tools used to
better quantify fracture risk and considers various clinical factors that may alter bone
quality.
Because DEXA is a two-dimensional technique, it cannot distinguish bone density of the
cortex from bone density at the trabecula. This technique also cannot distinguish
density-related osteoporosis from density changes related to arthritic changes, such as
osteophytes and degenerative sclerosis. In patients with severe degenerative disk
disease or hip joint arthritis, BMD measured via DEXA may be erroneously high because
of the bone proliferative changes associated with arthritis. Vertebral body compression
fractures, hip fractures, and implants also can affect BMD measurements via DEXA. In
patients with these findings, quantitative CT (QCT) may be helpful.
Serial DEXA
Serial BMD testing may aid in assessing a patient’s response to treatment or monitoring
progression of bone density loss.
Serial DEXA scans should be obtained at a single institution.

Serial DEXA
Repeat DEXA scans are warranted to monitor changes in BMD or to monitor treatment
response. For example, if BMD continues to decrease after the initiation of osteoporosis
management, then alternative treatment options should be considered.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
12/22

Serial DEXA scans usually are obtained every 2 years; however, DEXA may be repeated at
1 year if a change in treatment occurs or the patient has experienced a change in
medical status.
Not all DEXA scans are equivalent. DEXA scans from two different institutions cannot be
compared. Even within a single institution, BMD measurements may vary. Only DEXA
scans that have been obtained via machines that were cross-calibrated can be
compared.
Fracture Risk Assessment Tool
The FRAX helps determines the risk for fracture within 10 years.
The FRAX is based on age, sex, BMD, and various other clinical factors.
The FRAX is not validated in premenopausal women or in those with T-scores less than –2.5
(osteoporosis).

Fracture Risk Assessment Tool
The FRAX is a tool that calculates the risk for hip fracture or other major fracture within
10 years.10 The calculation considers age, sex, body habitus, and various other risk
factors that may affect bone density and bone quality. This tool has only been validated
for assessing risk in postmenopausal women or in men older than 50 years who have T-
scores between –1.0 and –2.5, meaning individuals with osteopenia or low BMD. If the
calculated risk for hip fracture is greater than or equal to 3% or if the risk for major hip
fracture is greater than or equal to 20%, then management is recommended.
Other Tools to Assess BMD and Osteoporosis
If DEXA cannot be performed, alternative methods can be used for BMD testing, including QCT
and quantitative ultrasonography.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
13/22

Other tools, such as vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) and trabecular bone score (TBS), can
be used in combination with DEXA to further quantify the risk for fracture.
Other Devices to Measure BMD
QCT is similar to DEXA in that images of the lumbar spine and the hip are used to determine
BMD.
QCT may be more effective in assessing BMD than DEXA in certain patient populations.
Finite element analysis (FEA) is a computer simulation that can be applied to QCT images to
assess bone strength.
Other devices include peripheral DEXA, peripheral QCT, and quantitative ultrasonography;
however, these are less commonly used.

Other Devices to Measure BMD
QCT is similar to DEXA but is obtained using a CT scanner (Figure 4). The CT scans are
select slices obtained through the lumbar spine (L1 through L4) and the pelvis. The QCT
is not a complete diagnostic CT scan of the lumbar spine and pelvis. Dissimilar from
DEXA, QCT is a three-dimensional imaging technique that can differentiate cortical bone
from trabecular bone.11 This is particularly helpful in patients with severe arthritis
because DEXA cannot distinguish altered bone density related to arthritis from that
related to osteoporosis. With QCT, a ROI is placed at the area to be measured. This ROI
may be purposefully placed to exclude certain areas, such as areas of severe arthritis.
Therefore, QCT also is helpful in individuals with implants or in other patients who are
unable to undergo DEXA, such as those with considerable scoliosis. In some individuals,
implant artifact is too extensive to allow for accurate measurement, even on QCT.
Surgeon should discuss these patients with the radiologist before imaging is performed.
The three-dimensional information available with QCT also may make this technique
more reliable than DEXA in evaluating osteoporosis in certain patient populations,
including individuals with spinal cord injury,12 men with chronic obstructive pulmonary
disease,13 and individuals being treated with long-term glucocorticoids.14

Figure 4 Quantitative axial (A), sagittal (B), and coronal (C) CT scans of the lumbar spine
of a postmenopausal woman with spinal implants. Axial images were reconstructed into
coronal and sagittal images to guide placement of the region of interest. The white
outlined oval on the axial CT scan is the region of interest within which bone mineral
density was measured. Any information outside the region of interest, including the
implants, was excluded from the measurement. (Courtesy of Rina Patel, MD, San
Francisco, CA.)
In addition to assessing BMD, QCT can be used to perform more complex analysis of
bone health. QCT scans can be used in computer programs that simulate the effect of
stress or load on an individual’s bone. This is called FEA. QCT-based FEA can be used to
estimate vertebral body and femoral strength and predict the risk for fractures at those
sites in postmenopausal women and older men. Although QCT with FEA is used for
research purposes, it also has clinical applications. QCT-based FEA can be used in clinical
settings to determine the timing of treatment initiation and to monitor
treatment.15 Although not equivalent to QCT or DEXA, measurement of low Hounsfield
units within the vertebral bodies on a diagnostic CT scan also has been correlated with
osteoporosis and fracture risk.16,17

Other devices include peripheral DEXA (DEXA performed at the forearm, phalanges, or
calcaneus), peripheral QCT (QCT at the distal radius or tibia), and quantitative
ultrasonography (ultrasonography at the calcaneus). In general, central DEXA is
preferred over these alternative methods. BMD measurements acquired via these
imaging modalities should be interpreted with caution. Recommendations for these
noncentral imaging modalities are outlined in the ISCD official positions.1
The BMD and T-scores calculated via non-DEXA imaging modalities are not necessarily
equivalent to those calculated via conventional DEXA. BMD measurements between
different imaging modalities cannot be accurately compared.
Vertebral Fracture Assessment
VFA is another tool for evaluating individuals with osteopenia or osteoporosis.
Compression fractures identified on VFA are graded according to the Genant classification.

Vertebral Fracture Assessment
VFA is a low-dose image of the thoracolumbar spine obtained via DEXA18 (Figure 5). It is
not equivalent to the diagnostic quality of a conventional radiograph; however, VFA is
adequate for assessing compression fractures and can be performed at the same time
as DEXA.
The Genant classification is used to quantify the severity of vertebral fractures. Less than
25% height loss is mild, between 25% and 40% height loss is moderate, and more than
40% height loss is severe.

patient with multiple compression fractures. Despite the low quality of the image,
fractures are visible at T11, L2, L3, and L4. The lowest height of each vertebral body (blue

Trabecular Bone Score
TBS is an analytic tool that evaluates the trabecular architecture of vertebral bodies via DEXA
scans.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:24 PM
AAOS | Imaging of Bone Mineral Density
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002057
17/22


Trabecular Bone Score
TBS uses texture analysis on lumbar spine DEXA scans to determine the trabecular
microarchitecture of the vertebral bodies19 (Figure 6). A low TBS is associated with
increased fracture risk. The TBS is used in combination with DEXA and FRAX to assess
future fracture risk; however, caution should be exercised in using TBS to monitor
treatment response. Although change in BMD after antiresorptive therapy has been
associated with a change in fracture risk, the same is not true for a change in TBS. The
role of TBS in monitoring response to management is unclear.20
